extracted.subtask_description: Crafting press releases that follow Associated Press (AP) style and formatting so they are clear, concise, and journalist-friendly. Covers punctuation, capitalization, numbers, formatting (headline, dateline, lead, body, boilerplate, media contact), quotes, fonts, and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow AP Stylebook rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An AP-style press release is written in the style of the Associated Press; follow AP Stylebook rules for punctuation, grammar and formatting to make your release appealing and easy for journalists to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following AP style demonstrates professionalism, improves readability and consistency, increases efficiency for journalists, and helps build better media relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxford comma
rubrics_metrics.description: AP style does not use the Oxford comma (also known as the serial comma) in a simple series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: write 'keynote speeches, panel discussions and networking opportunities' — not 'keynote speeches, panel discussions, and networking opportunities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single space after a period at the end of a sentence, not two spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to other sentence-ending punctuation (exclamation, question mark) as well; two spaces is a holdover from typewriters and is not used in modern digital press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks for direct quotes and single quotation marks for quotes within quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Our keynote speaker said, 'Innovation is the key to future success,' and I couldn't agree more," the CEO stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas in dates
rubrics_metrics.description: When a month and year are mentioned without a specific date, don’t use a comma; when a specific date is mentioned, set off the year with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example without specific date: 'The annual conference will be held in June 2024.' Example with date: 'The conference is scheduled for June 15, 2024.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens and dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens to link words that form a single modifier before a noun; use an em dash with a space on either side to signify a change or add emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphen example: 'cutting-edge technology.' Em dash formatting: use a spaced em dash to add emphasis or indicate a change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline capitalization (title case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use title case for headlines and subheads: capitalize the first word, the last word and all major words in between; lowercase minor words (articles, short prepositions, coordinating conjunctions) unless first or last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline: 'XYZ Corp Unveils New Tech at Annual Conference'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline capitalization and content
rubrics_metrics.description: In the dateline, the city name should be in all capital letters; include the state abbreviation for less well-known cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'CHICAGO, June 15, 2023 –' and 'MURRAY, Ky., June 15, 2023 –'. Dateline formatting should begin the first paragraph followed by an em dash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize formal titles when they appear before a name; lowercase them when they follow a name or are used alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'CEO Jane Smith announced...' but 'Jane Smith, chief executive officer, announced...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company and product name capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the capitalization style of company and product names, even if they don't follow standard capitalization rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use 'iPhone' or 'PayPal' as styled by the company; capitalize a proper noun at the beginning of a sentence even if it normally starts lowercase. If unsure, check authoritative sources (e.g., company website).

rubrics_metrics.name: General numbers rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers one through nine and use numerals for 10 and above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'nine keynote speakers and 15 breakout sessions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers exceptions (use numerals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always use numerals for ages, percentages, dimensions, temperatures, times, dates, monetary amounts and sports scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The 5-year-old company expects 20% growth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers at the beginning of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers at the beginning of a sentence, except for years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Fifty-two companies will exhibit...' but years (e.g., 2024) may start a sentence as numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinal numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out first through ninth and use numerals for 10th and above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'company's fourth annual conference and its 10th product launch.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Very large numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a combination of numerals and words for very large numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '1.5 million virtual attendees.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Font choice
rubrics_metrics.description: While AP style doesn't dictate specific fonts, use common, easily readable fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended fonts: Times New Roman, Arial or Calibri which render well across devices and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font size and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a font size between 10 and 12 points for body text and larger sizes for headlines; maintain consistency throughout the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines typically 14–16 points. Don't mix multiple fonts or sizes; inconsistent typography appears unprofessional and reduces readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bold or italics sparingly for emphasis and avoid underlining in digital formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underlining can be confused with hyperlinks online; avoid changing colors or fonts for emphasis unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes: attribution and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: On first reference, use the person's full name and title; afterward use only the last name. Keep periods and commas inside quotation marks; start a new paragraph for each new speaker; consider block quotes for quotes longer than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example attribution: '"This conference will be groundbreaking," said Jane Smith, CEO of XYZ Corp.' New paragraph per speaker improves clarity; indent long quotes as block quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline length and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep headlines under 100 characters if possible; be descriptive and specific and include the company name and the main news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report finding: headlines with 51–100 characters get the most views. Use strong, active verbs and appropriate tense (present for immediate news, future for upcoming events). Example: 'XYZ Corp Launches Innovative Tech Conference in Silicon Valley.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline should state location (city in caps, include state if needed) followed by the date and an em dash, placed at the beginning of the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'NEW YORK, June 15, 2023 –' or 'MANSFIELD, Mass., June 15, 2023 –'. The dateline gives context about where and when the news is coming from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory paragraph (lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph should summarize the whole news story and answer the '5 Ws' — who, what, when, where and why — putting the most newsworthy information first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in active voice, use strong verbs, and for event releases include event name, host, date and location. The dateline should precede the lead (see Dateline formatting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body text structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short paragraphs (typically 2–3 sentences), present information in descending order of importance, and intersperse relevant quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 300–500 words total for the release. Short paragraphs improve readability on mobile; most important details first (inverted pyramid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate content and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a standardized boilerplate about the company at the end of the press release, typically kept to 100 words or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boilerplate should include company mission, founding date, main products or services and significant achievements; place it just before media contact information and keep it consistent across releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide media contact details so journalists can follow up for more information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full name, title, phone number and email address. Example format: 'Media Contact: John Smith, PR Manager, XYZ Corp, 555-123-4567, [email protected]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required press release sections (AP-style format)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper AP-style press release includes these sections: headline, dateline, introductory paragraph (lead), body paragraphs, quotes, boilerplate and media contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each section follows the AP rules described in this guide for punctuation, capitalization, numbers, formatting and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and style: concise, journalist-friendly writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clearly, concisely and with respect for journalists' time; use active voice and strong verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep releases readable and scannable (short paragraphs, clear lead, descriptive headline) so journalists can quickly determine newsworthiness and repurpose content with minimal editing.
